[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 5.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"9a8c29","wall_time_seconds":0.4459616,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3683,"output":"</style>\\r\\n</head>\\r\\n<body>\\r\\n<main>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h1>Role Question Answer Choices (The Hardest Thing about Role Questions)</h1><div class=\\"source-note\\">Exercise format: each answer choice appears first as the question, followed immediately by its full breakdown and examples.</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>While the way in which we read the stimulus of any Role question is similar to how we approach Find the Conclusion questions, the answer choices we are faced with in Role questions are much more difficult. Life would be so simple if all the answer choices were just asking us if the statement in question is a premise or conclusion, but the test makers love to describe a relatively straightforward concept in abstract and vague language in Role question answer choices.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>As a result, the successful student should devote the majority of their time and energy to answer choices when approaching Role questions. As you get comfortable with analyzing the structure of the stimulus, it should become second nature to you. I use about 60% of all the time to examine answer choices in Role questions, with the other 40% set aside for reading the question and the stimulus.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>The ability to de-abstractify (translating vague and abstract terms that appear in answer choices into their stimulus equivalents) and knowing exactly what they are referring to is one of the most important skills that the advanced student needs to master. If you do not have this ability, often you will end up choosing a wrong answer choice even if you knew what you were looking for. You simply did not understand what the answer choice was trying to say. In other words, advanced students can read through a list of abstract answer choices and know exactly what they are referring to.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Take a look at the following answer choice examples, and see if you can decipher what is it that they are referring to, or even better, try to make up an argument with the components that would function as these answer choices describe:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 1</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It is used to illustrate the general principle that the argument presupposes</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Whenever we are faced with an answer choice that looks super abstract, the first thing to do is to always <strong>extract what keywords we can</strong> to try to make sense of the whole thing. Three words stand out in this answer choice: “illustrate”, “general principle”, and “presuppose”.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Now certain words have specific meanings within the LSAT. All three of these words appear repeatedly in LR questions and we need to memorize them:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Presuppose:</strong> in daily usage, a presupposition can mean either an assumption or something that is necessary. On the LSAT presuppose simply means “require”. (It’s talking about a necessary condition, something that we will soon cover.)</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Illustrate:</strong> an illustration, as it appears in a LR question, is simply referring to an example/examples</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>General Principle:</strong> we briefly touched upon the nature of principles on the LSAT in the last chapter, and will do so again further down the road. But for now, just know that a principle is a rule on what we should/shouldn’t do; and that it applies to multiple conditions and scenarios.</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>For example, “<em>John is always tired in the morning, he should go to bed earlier</em>” is not a principle, we are just talking about one person here. “<em>Those who are tired in the morning should strive to get to bed earlier</em>” is a principle. It’s no longer just about John anymore, it is a recommendation for a certain category of people.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So now there are three requirements that must be met if we were to select this hypothetical answer choice as the correct answer. First, the statement in question must be an example; second, behind this example is a principle on what we should or shouldn’t do; and lastly, this principle is required in order for the author to advance their argument.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Take a look at this example:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">Despite a high paying job, John was extremely stressed out and depressed</span>, so there are intangible things in life that we must pursue to find true happiness.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s situation is the illustration of a general principle; namely that having a lot of money isn’t enough to make you happy. Is this principle required in order for the conclusion to stand? Yes, the conclusion says factors other than money must be considered in order to be happy. The underlined statement satisfies all three requirements and if this was a Role question, this would be the correct answer.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n</section>\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 2</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Again, “<strong>Illustration</strong>” means example. So we know this answer choice is referring to an example in the stimulus. Furthermore, it is an illustration of a premise. So when examining this answer choice, we must isolate the premise/premises that appear in the argument and ask ourselves, is the quoted statement an example of what the premise is trying to say?</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>Here is an example to illustrate what this answer choice is trying to say:</strong></p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer.</span> Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer. We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>What is the premise here?</strong> Smoking causes lung cancer. <strong>What is the conclusion?</strong> Don’t smoke. John’s case is an illustration of the causal relationship between smoking and lung cancer. Requirement satisfied.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n</section>\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 3</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It is used to counter a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So right away, we should realize that “<em>a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</em>” is referring to a real or potential counter argument. A counter argument runs contrary to the author’s conclusion. If I say “going to college is a great way to enjoy a higher standard of living down the road,” but you respond with “but many college graduates have to take years to pay back debt”, you are making a counter argument in opposition to me.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Continuing with our example, if I had anticipated your potential objection/counter argument, I can say something along the lines of “college graduates enjoy higher income than their non college counterparts even with the cost of debt factored in.” What I’m doing, essentially, is anticipating your potential objection and shutting you down in advance. That’s what is meant by countering a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">College graduates make more money than they would if they didn’t go to college, even if they are paying off student loans plus interest.</span> So going to college is a great way to make more money and enjoy a better life.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here, the underlined statement is both a premise as well as a pre-emptive strike against a potential objection, namely that graduates end up with so much debt that going to college doesn’t make sense.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n</section>\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 4</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It makes an observation that, according to the argument, is insufficient to justify the claim that the argument concludes is false</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>A key piece of information we can extract from this answer choice is that there is a <em>claim that the argument concludes is false</em>. In other words, the author of this argument is arguing AGAINST a claim. Someone has made a claim, and the author is saying that claim is false.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So we have two viewpoints in this potential stimulus. The author’s argument is directed against an adversary.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Further, we know that the opponent made an observation in support of their view, but the author is saying that observation is not enough to prove anything, and subsequently goes on to argue that the opponent’s claim is false.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So in order for this answer choice to be correct, the stimulus must satisfy the following requirements: there must be an opposing view, the author must be arguing against this opposing view and declaring it false. The opponent must have provided an observation as a basis of support for their view, and the author must have made the claim that this observation is not enough to demonstrate the truth of the opponent’s view.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Let’s go a step further with a concrete example:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Celebrities have the biggest smiles in front of the camera</span>, so they must be the happiest people alive.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> That is not true. Many celebrities suffer from depression and substance abuse. Smiling in front of the camera doesn’t mean a thing, they could simply be putting on a show for the audience.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Does the underlined statement fit the requirement for this answer choice? Yes, David is arguing that John’s claim is false. David also suggests that the observation John makes in support of his claim is insufficient to justify his claim.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n</section>\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 5</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It describes a phenomenon for which the argument’s conclusion is offered as an explanation</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here is another key term that we must familiarize ourselves with: <strong>explanation</strong>.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Explanation: on the LSAT, the word “explanation” has a very strict and precise meaning, it simply means “cause.”</strong></div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So whenever you see the word “explanation” in an answer choice, check the stimulus for cause - effect reasoning. If it’s not there, then this answer would be wrong.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>What this answer choice is referring to is something we have seen before. We talked about questions where there is a cause and effect relationship in the argument, but instead of the cause being the premise and the effect being the conclusion, the order is reversed. The author describes a phenomenon and concludes what caused it. See PT43-S3-Q23 in the Find the Conclusion chapter if you had forgotten.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>We will reuse our example from the previous chapter:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">Smoking is a leading cause of lung cancer. <span class=\\"underlined\\">John has lung cancer</span>, therefore he must surely have been a heavy smoker.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John having lung cancer is the <strong>phenomenon</strong>, the author subsequently concludes that it must be smoking which caused his lung cancer. The cause - effect relationship goes like this: smoking → lung cancer, and the cause/explanation is in fact the conclusion in this example.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n</section>\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 6</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It is a general principle whose validity the argument questions</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Again, this answer choice is referring to a general principle, but it’s a general principle that the argument is questioning/attacking. So if we are confronted with this answer choice, we must go back to the stimulus to make sure it satisfies two requirements: one, the quoted statement is indeed a general principle; and two, the author is arguing against the truth of this principle. Here is an example that would match what this answer choice is saying:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">It has been said that <span class=\\"underlined\\">the best way to approach any situation is to be yourself</span>. But this cannot be true. What if you are a selfish, egotistical or horrible person? Surely we must strive to better ourselves and be the best we can be?</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n</section>\\r\\n<section class=\\"exercise\\"><div class=\\"exercise-label\\">Exercise 7</div><div class=\\"question-card\\"><div class=\\"question-label\\">Answer Choice</div><div class=\\"question-text\\">It denies a claim that the argument takes to be assumed in the reasoning it rejects</div></div><div class=\\"breakdown-label\\">Answer Choice Breakdown</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>This one is very similar to example 4. The argument is rejecting another person’s reasoning. So the author is arguing against someone else here. But are they rejecting that view outright? No, the author does something much more nuanced than that. The author thinks the reasoning used by their opponent has made an assumption, and instead of going after the opponent’s argument, our author is going after the opponent’s assumption.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So this answer choice is describing a stimulus in which there’s two arguments, the author’s argument and the opponent’s argument. This particular statement is the author rejecting an assumption made by the opponent’s argument.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>(We will look at the nature of assumptions in a subsequent chapter, as well as in Sufficient and Necessary Assumption question types.)</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> I’ve studied so hard for the finals, I’m definitely going to ace the exam!</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Studying hard doesn’t guarantee you will do well.</span> The exams are graded on a curve, and everyone else has studied just as hard.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}]

}\\r\\n</style>\\r\\n</head>\\r\\n<body>\\r\\n<main>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h1>Role Question Answer Choices (The Hardest Thing about Role Questions)</h1>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>While the way in which we read the stimulus of any Role question is similar to how we approach Find the Conclusion questions, the answer choices we are faced with in Role questions are much more difficult. Life would be so simple if all the answer choices were just asking us if the statement in question is a premise or conclusion, but the test makers love to describe a relatively straightforward concept in abstract and vague language in Role question answer choices.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>As a result, the successful student should devote the majority of their time and energy to answer choices when approaching Role questions. As you get comfortable with analyzing the structure of the stimulus, it should become second nature to you. I use about 60% of all the time to examine answer choices in Role questions, with the other 40% set aside for reading the question and the stimulus.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>The ability to de-abstractify (translating vague and abstract terms that appear in answer choices into their stimulus equivalents) and knowing exactly what they are referring to is one of the most important skills that the advanced student needs to master. If you do not have this ability, often you will end up choosing a wrong answer choice even if you knew what you were looking for. You simply did not understand what the answer choice was trying to say. In other words, advanced students can read through a list of abstract answer choices and know exactly what they are referring to.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Take a look at the following answer choice examples, and see if you can decipher what is it that they are referring to, or even better, try to make up an argument with the components that would function as these answer choices describe:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<ol class=\\"choice-list\\">\\r\\n<li>It is used to illustrate the general principle that the argument presupposes</li>\\r\\n<li>It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It is used to counter a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It makes an observation that, according to the argument, is insufficient to justify the claim that the argument concludes is false</li>\\r\\n<li>It describes a phenomenon for which the argument’s conclusion is offered as an explanation</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a general principle whose validity the argument questions</li>\\r\\n<li>It denies a claim that the argument takes to be assumed in the reasoning it rejects</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a claim for which no justification is provided but that is required to establish the argument’s main conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a claim for which justification is provided and that, if true, establishes the truth of the argument’s main conclusion</li>\\r\\n<li>It is what the author’s argument purports to explain</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a hypothesis that the argument attempts to undermine by calling into question the sufficiency of the evidence</li>\\r\\n<li>It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole but is not the only explicitly stated conclusion in the argument</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a statement that the argument is intended to support but is not the conclusion of the argument as a whole</li>\\r\\n<li>It is a statement for which some evidence is provided and that itself is offered as support for the conclusion of the argument as a whole</li>\\r\\n<li>It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole and is supported by another statement for which support is offered</li>\\r\\n</ol>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Yep, that was brutal. You probably had no idea what many of these even meant. Not to worry, let’s break them down one by one:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>1. It is used to illustrate the general principle that the argument presupposes</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Whenever we are faced with an answer choice that looks super abstract, the first thing to do is to always <strong>extract what keywords we can</strong> to try to make sense of the whole thing. Three words stand out in this answer choice: “illustrate”, “general principle”, and “presuppose”.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Now certain words have specific meanings within the LSAT. All three of these words appear repeatedly in LR questions and we need to memorize them:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Presuppose:</strong> in daily usage, a presupposition can mean either an assumption or something that is necessary. On the LSAT presuppose simply means “require”. (It’s talking about a necessary condition, something that we will soon cover.)</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Illustrate:</strong> an illustration, as it appears in a LR question, is simply referring to an example/examples</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>General Principle:</strong> we briefly touched upon the nature of principles on the LSAT in the last chapter, and will do so again further down the road. But for now, just know that a principle is a rule on what we should/shouldn’t do; and that it applies to multiple conditions and scenarios.</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>For example, “<em>John is always tired in the morning, he should go to bed earlier</em>” is not a principle, we are just talking about one person here. “<em>Those who are tired in the morning should strive to get to bed earlier</em>” is a principle. It’s no longer just about John anymore, it is a recommendation for a certain category of people.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So now there are three requirements that must be met if we were to select this hypothetical answer choice as the correct answer. First, the statement in question must be an example; second, behind this example is a principle on what we should or shouldn’t do; and lastly, this principle is required in order for the author to advance their argument.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Take a look at this example:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">Despite a high paying job, John was extremely stressed out and depressed</span>, so there are intangible things in life that we must pursue to find true happiness.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s situation is the illustration of a general principle; namely that having a lot of money isn’t enough to make you happy. Is this principle required in order for the conclusion to stand? Yes, the conclusion says factors other than money must be considered in order to be happy. The underlined statement satisfies all three requirements and if this was a Role question, this would be the correct answer.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>2. It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Again, “<strong>Illustration</strong>” means example. So we know this answer choice is referring to an example in the stimulus. Furthermore, it is an illustration of a premise. So when examining this answer choice, we must isolate the premise/premises that appear in the argument and ask ourselves, is the quoted statement an example of what the premise is trying to say?</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>Here is an example to illustrate what this answer choice is trying to say:</strong></p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer.</span> Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer. We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>What is the premise here?</strong> Smoking causes lung cancer. <strong>What is the conclusion?</strong> Don’t smoke. John’s case is an illustration of the causal relationship between smoking and lung cancer. Requirement satisfied.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>3. It is used to counter a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So right away, we should realize that “<em>a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion</em>” is referring to a real or potential counter argument. A counter argument runs contrary to the author’s conclusion. If I say “going to college is a great way to enjoy a higher standard of living down the road,” but you respond with “but many college graduates have to take years to pay back debt”, you are making a counter argument in opposition to me.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Continuing with our example, if I had anticipated your potential objection/counter argument, I can say something along the lines of “college graduates enjoy higher income than their non college counterparts even with the cost of debt factored in.” What I’m doing, essentially, is anticipating your potential objection and shutting you down in advance. That’s what is meant by countering a consideration that might be taken to undermine the argument’s conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">College graduates make more money than they would if they didn’t go to college, even if they are paying off student loans plus interest.</span> So going to college is a great way to make more money and enjoy a better life.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here, the underlined statement is both a premise as well as a pre-emptive strike against a potential objection, namely that graduates end up with so much debt that going to college doesn’t make sense.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>4. It makes an observation that, according to the argument, is insufficient to justify the claim that the argument concludes is false</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>A key piece of information we can extract from this answer choice is that there is a <em>claim that the argument concludes is false</em>. In other words, the author of this argument is arguing AGAINST a claim. Someone has made a claim, and the author is saying that claim is false.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So we have two viewpoints in this potential stimulus. The author’s argument is directed against an adversary.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Further, we know that the opponent made an observation in support of their view, but the author is saying that observation is not enough to prove anything, and subsequently goes on to argue that the opponent’s claim is false.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So in order for this answer choice to be correct, the stimulus must satisfy the following requirements: there must be an opposing view, the author must be arguing against this opposing view and declaring it false. The opponent must have provided an observation as a basis of support for their view, and the author must have made the claim that this observation is not enough to demonstrate the truth of the opponent’s view.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Let’s go a step further with a concrete example:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Celebrities have the biggest smiles in front of the camera</span>, so they must be the happiest people alive.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> That is not true. Many celebrities suffer from depression and substance abuse. Smiling in front of the camera doesn’t mean a thing, they could simply be putting on a show for the audience.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Does the underlined statement fit the requirement for this answer choice? Yes, David is arguing that John’s claim is false. David also suggests that the observation John makes in support of his claim is insufficient to justify his claim.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>5. It describes a phenomenon for which the argument’s conclusion is offered as an explanation</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here is another key term that we must familiarize ourselves with: <strong>explanation</strong>.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>Explanation: on the LSAT, the word “explanation” has a very strict and precise meaning, it simply means “cause.”</strong></div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So whenever you see the word “explanation” in an answer choice, check the stimulus for cause - effect reasoning. If it’s not there, then this answer would be wrong.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>What this answer choice is referring to is something we have seen before. We talked about questions where there is a cause and effect relationship in the argument, but instead of the cause being the premise and the effect being the conclusion, the order is reversed. The author describes a phenomenon and concludes what caused it. See PT43-S3-Q23 in the Find the Conclusion chapter if you had forgotten.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>We will reuse our example from the previous chapter:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">Smoking is a leading cause of lung cancer. <span class=\\"underlined\\">John has lung cancer</span>, therefore he must surely have been a heavy smoker.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John having lung cancer is the <strong>phenomenon</strong>, the author subsequently concludes that it must be smoking which caused his lung cancer. The cause - effect relationship goes like this: smoking → lung cancer, and the cause/explanation is in fact the conclusion in this example.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>6. It is a general principle whose validity the argument questions</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Again, this answer choice is referring to a general principle, but it’s a general principle that the argument is questioning/attacking. So if we are confronted with this answer choice, we must go back to the stimulus to make sure it satisfies two requirements: one, the quoted statement is indeed a general principle; and two, the author is arguing against the truth of this principle. Here is an example that would match what this answer choice is saying:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">It has been said that <span class=\\"underlined\\">the best way to approach any situation is to be yourself</span>. But this cannot be true. What if you are a selfish, egotistical or horrible person? Surely we must strive to better ourselves and be the best we can be?</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>7. It denies a claim that the argument takes to be assumed in the reasoning it rejects</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>This one is very similar to example 4. The argument is rejecting another person’s reasoning. So the author is arguing against someone else here. But are they rejecting that view outright? No, the author does something much more nuanced than that. The author thinks the reasoning used by their opponent has made an assumption, and instead of going after the opponent’s argument, our author is going after the opponent’s assumption.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So this answer choice is describing a stimulus in which there’s two arguments, the author’s argument and the opponent’s argument. This particular statement is the author rejecting an assumption made by the opponent’s argument.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>(We will look at the nature of assumptions in a subsequent chapter, as well as in Sufficient and Necessary Assumption question types.)</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>John:</strong> I’ve studied so hard for the finals, I’m definitely going to ace the exam!</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><strong>David:</strong> <span class=\\"underlined\\">Studying hard doesn’t guarantee you will do well.</span> The exams are graded on a curve, and everyone else has studied just as hard.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>8. It is a claim for which no justification is provided but that is required to establish the argument’s main conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>There are two important pieces of information in this answer choice that can help us determine whether it’s the correct answer. First, it is “required” to establish the argument’s main conclusion. That means it’s necessary in order for the main conclusion to be valid. So there’s no way this answer choice is talking about the conclusion itself, it’s therefore either a premise or an intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Second, the answer choice says it’s a claim for which no justification is provided. Remember what we said about how to differentiate between premises and intermediate conclusions in the previous chapter? Premises support the conclusion but do not have any other statements supporting them, whereas intermediate conclusions both support the conclusion and are supported by premises. So when we have a statement which supports the conclusion but is not supported by others, it can only mean one thing: we are talking about a premise here.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So we are essentially talking about a premise that is required to establish the truth of the conclusion. In other words, if the premise was untrue, the conclusion would not stand. Take a look at the following example for more clarity:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">I found an Olympic gold medal in the swim team locker room. It must have originally belonged to John. John is always losing things and <span class=\\"underlined\\">he participated in the Olympics.</span></p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s participation in the Olympics is a requirement for the example’s conclusion to stand. In order for John to be the original owner of the medal, he MUST have been a participant at least.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John’s participation in the Olympics is also a premise that supports the example argument’s conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>9. It is a claim for which justification is provided and that, if true, establishes the truth of the argument’s main conclusion</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Very similar to the example listed above, but with two important caveats. This answer choice HAS justification provided, while supporting the main conclusion, so it’s an intermediate conclusion. It also <strong>guarantees/establishes</strong> the truth of the conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">All practicing lawyers must have passed the bar. John is a partner at a prestigious law firm and therefore <span class=\\"underlined\\">he is a practicing lawyer</span>, so he must have passed the bar.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>John being a practicing lawyer is supported by the fact that he is a partner at a law firm. This satisfies the intermediate conclusion requirement. Does John being a practicing lawyer establish the fact that he has passed the bar? Yes, it is mentioned in the first statement/premise that all practicing lawyers must have passed the bar.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>10. It is what the author’s argument purports to explain</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>This is identical to example 5: the author describes an effect/result/phenomenon, and argues for a specific cause.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>11. It is a hypothesis that the argument attempts to undermine by calling into question the sufficiency of the evidence</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>What is a hypothesis?</strong> In science, a hypothesis is offered by scientists to try to explain a phenomenon in the physical world or universe. Why did different types of birds have physical features that are adapted to their physical environments? Darwin hypothesized that it is due to the fact that species can change over time, adapting to their environments via physical modifications generation after generation. Darwin came up with a hypothesis, which today we know as The Theory of Evolution, that has been supported by evidence gathered both by him and subsequent scientists. In other words, a hypothesis is simply a posited causal explanation of a phenomenon, explaining WHY something is the way it is.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"definition\\"><strong>On the LSAT, the word “hypothesis” can be understood as a “potential explanation/potential causation”; it usually appears in science/medicine themed LR stimuli.</strong></div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>So what is this answer choice saying? The argument is attempting to undermine this hypothesis. It does so by saying that the evidence out there is not enough to support such a hypothesis. So when we are going through answer choices and come to this, we must make sure that there is a hypothesis present in the stimulus (the quoted statement being that hypothesis), the author is challenging this hypothesis, and the author does so by suggesting that the available evidence is not enough to support this hypothesis.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>12. It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole but is not the only explicitly stated conclusion in the argument</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Two pieces of key information here. The first is straightforward: we are talking about the main conclusion here. But note that it “<em>is not the only explicitly stated conclusion in the argument</em>”. That can only mean one thing: we have an intermediate conclusion in the argument as well. So if confronted with this answer choice, make sure that one, the statement we are talking about is in fact the main conclusion of the argument; and two, the argument contains a separate intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>13. It is a statement that the argument is intended to support but is not the conclusion of the argument as a whole</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Something that is supported by the argument but is not the main conclusion, that’s an intermediate conclusion we are talking about here.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>14. It is a statement for which some evidence is provided and that itself is offered as support for the conclusion of the argument as a whole</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Same as above. The statement in question is supported by support, and supports the main conclusion. This is also the intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<h2>15. It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole and is supported by another statement for which support is offered</h2>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Same as example 12: the statement referred to by the answer choice is the main conclusion, and is supported by another statement for which support is offered. So the main conclusion is supported by an intermediate conclusion. When faced with an answer choice like this, make sure it is indeed the main conclusion that the question is asking us to analyze, and make sure the argument contains an intermediate conclusion.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"asterisk\\">***</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n</main>\\r\\n</body>\\r\\n</html>\\r\\n"}'}]

The statement about Maya illustrates that career success alone is not enough for happiness, which this argument requires.\n  - heading "The breakdown" [level=2]\n  - paragraph:\n    - text: Whenever we are faced with an answer choice that looks super abstract, the first thing to do is to always\n    - strong: extract what keywords we can\n    - text: "to try to make sense of the whole thing. Three words stand out in this answer choice: “illustrate”, “general principle”, and “presuppose”."\n  - paragraph: "Now certain words have specific meanings within the LSAT. All three of these words appear repeatedly in LR questions and we need to memorize them:"\n  - strong: "Presuppose:"\n  - text: in daily usage, a presupposition can mean either an assumption or something that is necessary. On the LSAT presuppose simply means “require”. (It’s talking about a necessary condition, something that we will soon cover.)\n  - strong: "Illustrate:"\n  - text: an illustration, as it appears in a LR question, is simply referring to an example/examples\n  - strong: "General Principle:"\n  - text: we briefly touched upon the nature of principles on the LSAT in the last chapter, and will do so again further down the road. But for now, just know that a principle is a rule on what we should/shouldn’t do; and that it applies to multiple conditions and scenarios.\n  - paragraph:\n    - text: For example, “\n    - emphasis: John is always tired in the morning, he should go to bed earlier\n    - text: ” is not a principle, we are just talking about one person here. “\n    - emphasis: Those who are tired in the morning should strive to get to bed earlier\n    - text: ” is a principle. It’s no longer just about John anymore, it is a recommendation for a certain category of people.\n  - paragraph: So now there are three requirements that must be met if we were to select this hypothetical answer choice as the correct answer. First, the statement in question must be an example; second, behind this example is a principle on what we should or shouldn’t do; and lastly, this principle is required in order for the author to advance their argument.\n  - paragraph: "Take a look at this example:"\n  - paragraph: Despite a high paying job, John was extremely stressed out and depressed, so there are intangible things in life that we must pursue to find true happiness.\n  - paragraph: John’s situation is the illustration of a general principle; namely that having a lot of money isn’t enough to make you happy. Is this principle required in order for the conclusion to stand? Yes, the conclusion says factors other than money must be considered in order to be happy. The underlined statement satisfies all three requirements and if this was a Role question, this would be the correct answer.\n  - paragraph: Compare your work with the breakdown. Your responses are saved as practice, without a correctness score.\n  - button "Next answer choice"'}]

Never invent a link target and leave it missing without labeling it as a gap.\\r\\n\\r\\nNew compiled knowledge pages use this minimal frontmatter, extending the existing `type`, `subject`, `updated`, and `aliases` convention:\\r\\n\\r\\n```yaml\\r\\n---\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\nsubject: Compiled knowledge\\r\\ncreated: 2026-09-30\\r\\nupdated: 2026-09-30\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\ntags: [llm-wiki]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../sources/llm-wiki-pattern.md\\r\\n---\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nChoose an appropriate type such as `source`, `entity`, `concept`, `comparison`, or `synthesis`. `sources` contains relative links to supporting source summaries or evidence, not unverified attribution. Add a verification date and live-system name in the body when operational facts need freshness. Existing pages need not be retrofitted just to satisfy this template; preserve their metadata and domain conventions when editing.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis human-directed editing schema does not grant automated overwrite permissions. [The automation metadata schema](frontmatter.md) remains authoritative for `brain-managed`, `schema-version`, and `domain`. Do not add `brain-managed: true` to ordinary pages by default. Unattended automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections and uses compare-and-swap.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach source summary contains:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Source identity: title, author if known, original URL or supplied fi…532 tokens truncated….\\r\\n2. Compute the source hash and compare available provenance or summaries for an identical source. Identical bytes do not need a second summary. A changed version keeps its own provenance and an explicit relationship to the earlier generation. Do not equate similar titles with identical contents.\\r\\n3. Copy evidence into the archive and verify hashes before compiling. Preserve originals. A processed inbox item may be recorded as processed without deletion; moving or deleting needs explicit authorization.\\r\\n4. Read the complete relevant source. For meaningful images, inspect them separately where supported; do not claim to have understood images from Markdown alt text alone.\\r\\n5. Present key takeaways and the pages they would affect. Default to one source at a time with Joshua involved. If he explicitly asks to implement the supplied source, this authorizes that source\'s integration without an extra approval loop; make routine filing choices and report them. Batch intake requires an explicit batch request.\\r\\n6. Write or update the source summary. Update relevant existing entities, concepts, domain records, comparisons, and synthesis. Preserve qualifications and explain changed conclusions. A source may touch 10–15 pages; that is a possibility, never a quota. Touch only pages whose content or useful connections actually change.\\r\\n7. Update the relevant indexes and reciprocal links. Record contradictory evidence with links to both claims and their dates. Leave the conflict explicitly unresolved until evidence or Joshua adjudicates it; do not silently replace one generation with another.\\r\\n8. Verify edited-page links, evidence paths and hashes, index entries, and the completeness of the intended changes. Append the ingest log entry and report what changed, what remains unresolved, and anything skipped.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first worked example is [the idea file\'s source summary](../../wiki/sources/llm-wiki-pattern.md), connected to [compiled knowledge](../../wiki/concepts/compiled-knowledge.md) and this operating schema. It illustrates source evidence, attributed summary, local synthesis, cross-links, index entries, and a dated ingest log without treating every claim in the idea file as proven.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Query starts with the index and compounds useful answers\\r\\n\\r\\nFor knowledge-bearing interactions, resolve the owning domain. Read `wiki/hot.md` when current-session context matters, then the appropriate index and linked pages. For a wiki query, the index comes before ad hoc searching raw files. Use `rg` to resolve omissions or scale limits, and escalate to a relevant source or live system when the compiled pages lack evidence or freshness.\\r\\n\\r\\nAnswer in plain language with links to the pages and evidence used. State uncertainty and unresolved conflicts. If the answer changes durable understanding, update its existing authoritative page. Create a new comparison or synthesis page only when it has a distinct lasting purpose; link it from the index and supporting pages. File useful findings, not every conversational sentence. Record filed query outputs in the log.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe schema applies to knowledge intake, questions, decisions, drafting, and maintenance. Mechanical shell/Git/file operations, self-contained code edits, and narrow skill inputs need not read the wiki merely to satisfy a ritual. A brief transient question does not require a new page or log entry. Do not use the schema to send messages, change a live backend, deploy, delete, or expose credentials outside existing authorization.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The index catalogs content; the log records changes\\r\\n\\r\\n`wiki/index.md` is the master content catalog. List every wiki page once in the complete catalog under a useful category (curated navigation links may also point to those pages) with a working link and one-line description. Include navigation links to `corpus/index.md`, `students/README.md`, this schema, and other authoritative external homes rather than flattening their full contents into the wiki index. Useful categories include hubs, entities, concepts, source summaries, comparisons/synthesis, operations, and references. Dates and source counts are optional; if present, keep them accurate. Update the index on every ingest and whenever pages or their purpose change. Run `py system/scripts/wiki-maintenance.py --index` to refresh its fenced generated catalog without replacing curated navigation; the script checks for concurrent edits before writing.\\r\\n\\r\\n`wiki/log.md` is append-only. Preserve old entries even when a conclusion changes; append a correction or superseding entry. New entries use:\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n## [2026-09-30] ingest | LLM Wiki pattern\\r\\n\\r\\n- Source: [source summary](sources/llm-wiki-pattern.md); provenance and SHA-256 linked there.\\r\\n- Changed: source summary, compiled-knowledge concept, operating schema, and index.\\r\\n- Finding: compile source knowledge into maintained linked pages; preserve current domain homes.\\r\\n- Verification: evidence hash, links, and index entries checked.\\r\\n- Open: any unresolved conflict or gap, or \\"None\\".\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nUse operation names `ingest`, `query`, `lint`, or `system`. Include source/output links, meaningful changed pages, findings, verification, and unresolved work as relevant. Absolute dates use Joshua\'s client timezone. A log is not a copied transcript, a credential store, or a substitute for `wiki/tasks.md`. Log locked decisions in `decisions/log.md` as well when the task actually locks a decision.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Lint keeps the compiled knowledge trustworthy\\r\\n\\r\\nRun a focused consistency check after each ingest or durable query edit. Run a broader lint when Joshua asks, after a substantial batch or structural change, or when retrieval exposes contradictions or broken navigation. Periodically suggest a wider check when the vault has accumulated unchecked changes; no scheduled automation is implied.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead large indexes through curated navigation and bounded catalog searches, not whole-file dumps. Before calling knowledge ingestion finished, test one natural retrieval question through the relevant index/domain hub to a compiled page with evidence. Copying a source or adding a catalog entry alone is not sufficient.\\r\\n\\r\\nRun `py system/scripts/wiki-maintenance.py --lint` for structural checks; results go to `system/generated/wiki-lint.generated.tsv`. This checks local links, source metadata, and possible orphans. It does not establish semantic truth, freshness, or completeness.\\r\\n\\r\\nInspect contradictory claims, facts superseded by newer evidence, stale operational snapshots, orphan pages without useful inbound links, missing targets, missing reciprocal links, concepts that merit a page, duplicate subject pages, absent provenance, and evidence gaps. Report each finding with affected links, why it matters, and a recommended correction or research question. Fix clear reversible link/index errors within authorized scope. Keep interpretive conflicts explicit and ask Joshua only where his judgment is required. Do not invent fresh evidence or silently merge incompatible claims. Append a lint entry with scope, fixes, unresolved findings, and verification limits.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Tools improve the workflow without becoming requirements\\r\\n\\r\\nMarkdown files, working links, the index, the log, and existing Git history are sufficient to start. Obsidian can browse pages and show the graph. Web Clipper can place new captures in the inbox. Locally stored attachments may make evidence more durable; inspect images explicitly and preserve provenance. Dataview, Marp, plots, canvases, or slide decks are optional output formats. A local search tool such as qmd is an option only if index navigation and ordinary text search cease to be adequate.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not install any tool or plugin merely to implement the pattern. Use existing connected capabilities and applicable skills. Protect exclusions before a Git commit or push; Markdown version history must not drag raw personal exports, credentials, or nested app repositories into the outer repository.\\r\\n"}'}]

It supersedes the guided choice-1 proposal and conditional lecture ending farther below. The lesson uses source choice 2 because its example shows the example-to-premise-to-conclusion relationship directly. No new scenarios are invented.\\r\\n\\r\\nPlacement: keep the Desktop source’s four introduction paragraphs exactly; follow them with the opening and guided example below. Keep the fifteen original choices/breakdowns exact and in order. Place the closing after the fifteenth original breakdown. No additional required modules are proposed. Source introduction/breakdown HTML remains untouched.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Draft opening and guided source example\\r\\n\\r\\n### An answer choice describes a relationship\\r\\n\\r\\nAn abstract answer choice tells us what a statement does in an argument. To understand it, we need more than the name of a role. We need to see the relationship the choice describes.\\r\\n\\r\\nA premise is a reason for accepting a conclusion. An example can illustrate that premise. Those are related jobs, but they are different jobs. The answer choice can ask us to follow both.\\r\\n\\r\\nConsider this original choice:\\r\\n\\r\\n> It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion\\r\\n\\r\\n**Illustration** means an example. **Premise** tells us that the idea being illustrated is a reason the author uses. **Support the argument’s conclusion** tells us what that reason is used for.\\r\\n\\r\\nSo there are two relationships to check: the statement must be an example of the premise, and the premise must support the conclusion. Calling the statement “an example” gets us started. It does not finish the work.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Follow the original example\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is the original source example, unchanged. The underlined statement is the one the choice describes:\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\"><span class=\\"underlined\\">John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer.</span> Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer. We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst, find the point the author wants us to accept. Here, the author says we must avoid cigarettes if we want to stay healthy.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhat reason does the author give? **Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer.** That is the premise used to support the recommendation.\\r\\n\\r\\nNow look at the underlined statement. John smoked two packs a day and was diagnosed with lung cancer. The source presents John’s case as an example of the causal relationship stated in the premise.\\r\\n\\r\\nWe can now follow the whole description. **John’s case illustrates the premise. The premise supports the conclusion.** The choice describes what the underlined statement does, including the connection to the reason and the reason’s connection to the final point.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf we only noticed that the paragraph discusses smoking, we would miss the structure. If we only noticed that John’s case is an example, we would leave part of the choice unchecked. We need to know what it is an example of and how that idea is used in the argument.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis explains the source example’s role. It does not ask us to decide whether the argument has proved its causal claim. The task here is to understand the description and identify the relationship the source is showing.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Make each choice concrete\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each of the fifteen choices, there are two pieces of written work you can use to test your understanding.\\r\\n\\r\\n**State the requirements.** What would have to appear in an argument for the choice to describe it correctly? Keep every part of the description. A claim receiving support is different from a claim receiving no justification. A claim being required is different from a claim establishing the conclusion.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Create an example argument.** Write reasons and a conclusion, then identify the particular statement the choice would describe. Check where each requirement appears in your example. If one part is missing, you know what still needs work.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe original breakdown is available whenever you need it. You can try the written work first, open the explanation to learn the relationship, or return to revise your example after reading. Reading the breakdown and completing the written work are recorded separately.\\r\\n\\r\\nAs you continue, keep comparing the wording of the choice with what the statement actually does. The explanation should make the language more concrete. Your example gives you a chance to use that meaning yourself.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Draft closing after the fifteenth exact breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check the whole description\\r\\n\\r\\nThe fifteen choices use different words, but the task stays the same: turn the description into requirements you can check.\\r\\n\\r\\nStart with the idea the choice names. Is it an example, a principle, an observation, a hypothesis, or a conclusion? Then look at what happens to that idea. Is it used as support, challenged, denied, or offered as an explanation?\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the strength of the wording. **Required** and **establishes** do different work. **Attempts** does not tell us that the attempt succeeds. **Explicitly stated** asks for something the argument actually says. Leaving out one of these details changes the description you are trying to satisfy.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe final choices also show why we trace each link of support. A statement can receive support and then support the main conclusion. Or it can be the main conclusion, supported by another statement that itself receives support. Ask why we should believe each claim and look for the reason the argument gives. Then ask what that claim supports in turn.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou can return to any choice and check your own example against its original breakdown. Have you included every required part? Have you identified the statement the choice describes? Does that statement actually do what the full choice says?\\r\\n\\r\\nThat completes this lecture. When you later meet this language in a full LSAT question, look for those same parts and relationships in the argument you are given.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source map for this ready copy\\r\\n\\r\\n- Desktop `role_question_answer_choices_complete_transcription.html`: exact choice 2 and its complete example paragraph; breakdown 2 identifies smoking/causation as the premise and avoiding cigarettes as the conclusion. Source example 8 assumes Olympic participation is required for original ownership of the medal; retained as authored, not strengthened into a universal fact. Source explanations of hypothesis/explanation use the course’s causal sense. No new practice scenarios were invented.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Definitions needing approval\\r\\n\\r\\n- **support**: Give a reason to accept a claim.\\r\\n- **conclusion**: A claim the author supports with reasons.\\r\\n- **counter**: Answer or oppose a point against the argument.\\r\\n- **consideration**: A point that could count against the conclusion in this choice.\\r\\n- **might**: Could; the choice allows a possible objection.\\r\\n- **observation**: Something noticed or reported about the world.\\r\\n- **insufficient**: Not enough to establish the claim.\\r\\n- **justify**: Provide enough reason to accept a claim.\\r\\n- **claim**: A statement put forward as true.\\r\\n- **false**: Untrue.\\r\\n- **phenomenon**: The event, effect, or situation being explained.\\r\\n- **validity**: Whether the principle is true or acceptable in this choice.\\r\\n- **questions**: Challenges or calls into doubt.\\r\\n- **denies**: Says a claim is not true.\\r\\n- **assumed**: Taken for granted without being established.\\r\\n- **reasoning**: The way reasons are used to support a claim.\\r\\n- **rejects**: Refuses to accept.\\r\\n- **no justification**: No supporting reason for this claim is supplied in the argument.\\r\\n- **required**: Necessary for this argument; meeting it may not be enough.\\r\\n- **establish**: Secure the conclusion, rather than merely make it more likely.\\r\\n- **justification**: A reason supplied to support a claim.\\r\\n- **if true**: The stated result follows on the condition that the claim is true.\\r\\n- **establishes**: Secures the conclusion, rather than merely makes it more likely.\\r\\n- **purports**: Claims or attempts to do something, without saying it succeeds.\\r\\n- **attempts**: Tries to; success is not asserted.\\r\\n- **sufficiency**: Whether something is enough.\\r\\n- **evidence**: Information offered as support for a claim.\\r\\n- **as a whole**: Considering the complete argument and its final point.\\r\\n- **not the only**: There is at least one other.\\r\\n- **explicitly stated**: Said directly in the argument, rather than left unstated.\\r\\n- **intended**: Meant to do something.\\r\\n- **not the conclusion**: Does not function as the final point of the complete argument.\\r\\n- **provided**: Given within the argument.\\r\\n- **supported**: Given reasons or evidence to accept it.\\r\\n- **offered**: Presented for the stated purpose.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Inherited definitions\\r\\n\\r\\n- **illustrate**: Give an example.\\r\\n- **general principle**: A rule about what should or shouldn\'t be done that covers many cases.\\r\\n- **presupposes**: Require.\\r\\n- **illustration**: An example.\\r\\n- **premise**: A reason the author gives to support a conclusion.\\r\\n- **undermine**: Weaken. Push against.\\r\\n- **explanation**: Give the cause.\\r\\n- **main conclusion**: The final point the author wants you to accept.\\r\\n- **explain**: Give the cause.\\r\\n- **hypothesis**: A possible explanation: a proposed cause.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Choice 1\\r\\n\\r\\nSource exercise 1; walkthrough and meaning pending approval.\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}]

Why Abstract Is Hard":\n      - generic: M1. Why Abstract Is Hard\n    - button "M2. LSAT Words You Must Know":\n      - generic: M2. LSAT Words You Must Know\n    - button "M3. Break It Down":\n      - generic: M3. Break It Down\n    - button "Reference":\n      - text: Reference\n- main:\n  - button "Module 1":\n    - text: Module 1\n  - \'heading "Note: Why Abstract Answer Choices Feel Hard" [level=2]\'\n  - paragraph: What an abstract answer choice is, and why it reads like a riddle.\n  - article:\n    - paragraph: While the way in which we read the stimulus of any Role question is similar to how we approach Find the Conclusion questions, the answer choices we are faced with in Role questions are much more difficult. Life would be so simple if all the answer choices were just asking us if the statement in question is a premise or conclusion, but the test makers love to describe a relatively straightforward concept in abstract and vague language in Role question answer choices.\n    - paragraph: As a result, the successful student should devote the majority of their time and energy to answer choices when approaching Role questions. As you get comfortable with analyzing the structure of the stimulus, it should become second nature to you. I use about 60% of all the time to examine answer choices in Role questions, with the other 40% set aside for reading the question and the stimulus.\n    - paragraph: The ability to de-abstractify (translating vague and abstract terms that appear in answer choices into their stimulus equivalents) and knowing exactly what they are referring to is one of the most important skills that the advanced student needs to master. If you do not have this ability, often you will end up choosing a wrong answer choice even if you knew what you were looking for. You simply did not understand what the answer choice was trying to say. In other words, advanced students can read through a list of abstract answer choices and know exactly what they are referring to.\n    - paragraph: "Take a look at the following answer choice examples, and see if you can decipher what is it that they are referring to, or even better, try to make up an argument with the components that would function as these answer choices describe:"\n    - region "An answer choice describes a relationship":\n      - heading "An answer choice describes a relationship" [level=2]\n      - paragraph: An abstract answer choice tells us what a statement does in an argument. To understand it, we need more than the name of a role. We need to see the relationship the choice describes.\n      - paragraph: A premise is a reason for accepting a conclusion. An example can illustrate that premise. Those are related jobs, but they are different jobs. The answer choice can ask us to follow both.\n      - paragraph: "Consider this original choice:"\n      - blockquote: It is an illustration of a premise that is used to support the argument’s conclusion\n      - paragraph:\n        - strong: Illustration\n        - text: means an example.\n        - strong: Premise\n        - text: tells us that the idea being illustrated is a reason the author uses.\n        - strong: Support the argument’s conclusion\n        - text: tells us what that reason is used for.\n      - paragraph: "So there are two relationships to check: the statement must be an example of the premise, and the premise must support the conclusion. Calling the statement “an example” gets us started. It does not finish the work."\n      - heading "Follow the original example" [level=3]\n      - paragraph: "The following is the original source example, unchanged. The underlined statement is the one the choice describes:"\n      - paragraph: John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer. Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer. We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.\n      - paragraph: First, find the point the author wants us to accept. Here, the author says we must avoid cigarettes if we want to stay healthy.\n      - paragraph:\n        - text: What reason does the author give?\n        - strong: Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer.\n        - text: That is the premise used to support the recommendation.\n      - paragraph: Now look at the underlined statement. John smoked two packs a day and was diagnosed with lung cancer. The source presents John’s case as an example of the causal relationship stated in the premise.\n      - paragraph:\n        - text: We can now follow the whole description.\n        - strong: John’s case illustrates the premise. The premise supports the conclusion.\n        - text: The choice describes what the underlined statement does, including the connection to the reason and the reason’s connection to the final point.\n      - figure "John’s case illustrates the premise, which supports the conclusion":\n        - paragraph: The example\n        - paragraph: John has been smoking two packs a day since he was sixteen, last week he was diagnosed with lung cancer.\n        - generic: illustrates\n        - paragraph: The premise\n        - paragraph: Smoking is a direct cause of lung cancer.\n        - generic: supports\n        - paragraph: The conclusion\n        - paragraph: We must avoid cigarettes at all costs if we want to stay healthy.\n      - paragraph: If we only noticed that the paragraph discusses smoking, we would miss the structure. If we only noticed that John’s case is an example, we would leave part of the choice unchecked. We need to know what it is an example of and how that idea is used in the argument.\n      - paragraph: This explains the source example’s role. It does not ask us to decide whether the argument has proved its causal claim. The task here is to understand the description and identify the relationship the source is showing.\n    - heading "Answer Choice Traps" [level=1]\n    - generic: Answer Choice Type 1\n    - heading "Half right half wrong answers" [level=2]\n    - paragraph:\n      - strong: An essential habit to have for the hardest LR questions (and RC questions) is to carefully parse the answer choices, looking for suspicious keywords or concepts and connections that seem out of place.\n    - paragraph: The test makers love to offer us an answer choice that is only partially correct. The first half of the answer may be correct, but the second half will contain out of scope information, for instance. So it’s crucial to review each answer word by word, looking for red flags.\n    - generic: Answer Choice Type 2\n    - heading "Answers describing something that did not happen" [level=2]\n    - paragraph: For questions whose correct answer describes a feature of the stimuli’s argument (Role, Method, Flaw), we need to keep a watchful eye for answer choices describing something that does not happen in the argument.\n    - paragraph: In fact, identifying answer choices that deviate from the stimulus is a sure-fire way to eliminate erroneous contenders from the selection. For these four types of questions, read the answer choice, think about what it means, isolate any suspicious words in them, and ask yourself, “does the author do this in their argument?”\n    - paragraph: But of course, this depends on the question type we are working on. Similar to Out of Scope answer choices, answer choices describing something that does not occur in the stimulus can work as correct Strengthen/Weaken answers, among others.\n    - generic: Answer Choice Type 3\n    - heading "Answer choices that are too vague/abstract" [level=2]\n    - paragraph: Finally, we have seen how the correct answer can be vaguely worded. We have even practiced the art of extrapolating what an answer is referring to by analyzing its keywords.\n    - paragraph: Extracting certain keywords from vague or abstract answer choices in order to understand what that answer choice is actually talking about is also an invaluable skill. Unfortunately, it’s one of the most under-developed skills and often overlooked when students pursue speed at the expense of accuracy.\n    - paragraph: Lastly, a common trick employed by the authors of the test is to have an almost perfect answer with a glaring error, usually due to one single word placed right next to the correct answer, which is worded vaguely. This is a trap that we shall see over and over again throughout the book.\n  - button "I read this":\n    - text: I read this\n  - generic: Click when done'}]

Its snapshot is dated 2026-08-03; this is source evidence, not a current live-backend check.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Module 4 draft: match every requirement to the argument\\r\\n\\r\\nPurpose: move from describing what an answer needs to pointing to the actual parts of one full source argument. Unlike Module 3’s learner-created examples, this lesson supplies the argument and asks the learner to locate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### A description has to fit this argument\\r\\n\\r\\nAn answer choice can sound familiar and still describe the wrong relationship.
